lesson.title: A neural net from scratch

primer.title: A neuron holds a number
primer.body: The input neuron holds x. Each hidden neuron holds a number between -1 and 1, its activation, computed from the layer before it. The output neuron holds the network's answer, y.

primer.title: Weights and a bias
primer.body: Each connection multiplies the signal by a weight: positive pushes the next neuron up, negative pushes it down. The bias shifts where the neuron switches on.

primer.title: tanh bends
primer.body: tanh squishes any total into -1..1. Stacking these bends is what lets the network draw a curve; the output skips tanh, so it can answer any number.

primer.title: Learning goes downhill
primer.body: The loss says how wrong the outputs are. Backprop finds which way each weight should move to lower it, and each training step moves it a little that way.

lesson.overview: We'll build a neural network with nothing but NumPy and teach it to draw a curve: y = sin(x) for x from -π to π. One input (x), two hidden layers of 4 neurons, one output (y). First the network and its forward pass, then backprop, then a training loop, and last a test that prints -1, 0, 1 for -π/2, 0, π/2.

build.summary: A 1-4-4-1 neural network in NumPy that learns y = sin(x).
build.outcome: Run it and the loss falls below 0.01; it prints [-1.0, 0.0, 1.0] for x = -π/2, 0, π/2.

payload.title: Build the network
payload.instructions: In nn.py, paste this under # The network
payload.details: Under # The network, add the data (y = sin(x)), the weights and the forward pass.
payload.what: The sine data, random weights and a forward pass
payload.why: Every guess the network makes is this forward pass: x goes through two layers of tanh neurons, and the output neuron adds them up into y.
payload.code:
X = np.linspace(-np.pi, np.pi, 50).reshape(-1, 1)
y = np.sin(X)

np.random.seed(0)
W1 = np.random.randn(1, 4)
b1 = np.zeros((1, 4))
W2 = np.random.randn(4, 4)
b2 = np.zeros((1, 4))
W3 = np.random.randn(4, 1) * 0.1
b3 = np.zeros((1, 1))

def forward(X):
    h1 = np.tanh(X @ W1 + b1)
    h2 = np.tanh(h1 @ W2 + b2)
    return h1, h2, h2 @ W3 + b3

payload.label: nn.py creates W1, W2 and W3
nn.py defines forward with two tanh layers

payload.caption: What you're building: x goes in, y comes out. Brightness is a neuron's activation; blue weights push up, brown push down.

payload.instructions: In nn.py, paste backward under # Backprop
payload.details: Under # Backprop, add backward. It returns one gradient per weight and bias.
payload.what: A gradient for every weight, with the chain rule
payload.why: The chain rule sends the output's error back one layer at a time, so each weight learns its share of the blame.

payload.label: nn.py sends the error back through W3 and W2

payload.caption: Backprop: the output's error flows back along the same weights, and each weight gets its share.

payload.label: nn.py sends the error back through W3 and W2

payload.title: Write the training loop
payload.instructions: In nn.py, paste the loop under # Training
payload.details: Under # Training, add the training loop. It prints the loss every 2,000 epochs.
payload.what: A loop that steps every weight downhill 20,000 times
payload.why: Each step lowers the loss a little. The loop prints the loss every 2,000 epochs so you can watch it fall.
payload.code:
lr = 0.1
for epoch in range(20000):
    h1, h2, out = forward(X)
    dW3, db3, dW2, db2, dW1, db1 = backward(X, y, h1, h2, out)
    W3 -= lr * dW3
    b3 -= lr * db3
    W2 -= lr * dW2
    b2 -= lr * db2
    W1 -= lr * dW1
    b1 -= lr * db1
    loss = np.mean((out - y) ** 2)
    if epoch % 2000 == 0:
        print(f"epoch {epoch:5d}  loss {loss:.4f}")

payload.label: nn.py updates W1, W2 and W3

payload.caption: What your loop will do: every weight takes a small step downhill 20,000 times, and y settles on sin(x).

payload.title: What a neuron does
payload.body: It adds its inputs, each times a weight, plus a bias, then tanh squishes the total into -1..1. That number is how lit up it is. The output neuron skips tanh, so it can answer any number.

payload.title: Why no tanh on the output?
payload.body: tanh keeps a neuron between -1 and 1. The hidden layers need that bend; the output just adds them up, so it can reach any value. Its weights start small (* 0.1), so its first guesses are near 0.

payload.caption: What you're building: x goes in, y comes out. Brightness is a neuron's activation; blue weights push up, brown push down.

payload.title: Hint 1 of 2
payload.body: Start at the output: d_out is how wrong it was. The output has no tanh, so there is no slope to multiply.

payload.title: How backprop assigns blame
payload.body: Start at the output: how wrong was it? Each weight into it is blamed by how much it contributed. Then do the same one layer back, and once more.

payload.title: Why 1 - h2 ** 2?
payload.body: It's tanh's slope. The chain rule multiplies it in wherever the signal went through a tanh.

payload.caption: Backprop: the output's error flows back along the same weights, and each weight gets its share.

payload.title: One pass of the loop
payload.body: forward makes a guess for all 50 points, backward says which way each weight should move, and each weight moves a little that way (lr sets how far). 20,000 times.

payload.title: Why lr = 0.1?
payload.body: Small enough that each step doesn't overshoot, big enough to finish in a second. Real networks tune it the same way: try a few and watch the loss.

payload.caption: What your loop will do: every weight takes a small step downhill 20,000 times, and y settles on sin(x).

payload.title: Why zeros can't learn
payload.body: With every weight at 0, all eight hidden neurons output tanh(0) = 0, so the network answers 0 for every x. Every weight's gradient is exactly zero, so they stay copies and nothing moves.

payload.title: What the weights mean
payload.body: Each first-layer neuron is tanh(w·x), an S-curve through 0: steep when its weight is big, gentle when it's small. The second layer mixes those S-curves, and the output adds them up into the sine wave. The biases stay at 0: sin is symmetric (sin(-x) = -sin(x)), and so is a network with no biases.

payload.title: What next?
payload.body: Swap np.sin for another curve, like np.cos, and train again: the same network and the same four pieces learn it.
